Factorial designs are especially useful when interactions between variables are expected or unknown.

Each method should, in theory, yield the same GDP figure, providing a comprehensive picture of economic activity from different angles. Understanding these approaches helps us appreciate the complexity behind national income accounting.

Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods are essential computational tools that allow hierarchical Bayesian models to approximate complex posterior distributions when analytical solutions are infeasible. MCMC generates a sequence of samples from the posterior distribution by constructing a Markov chain that, over time, converges to the target distribution. This convergence ensures that the samples accurately represent the underlying probabilities. Techniques like the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm or Gibbs sampling guide this process, balancing exploration and exploitation of the parameter space. To assess accuracy and convergence, economists use diagnostic tools such as trace plots, autocorrelation checks, and convergence statistics like the Gelman-Rubin statistic. These diagnostics help confirm that the chain has stabilized and that estimates are reliable. By enabling efficient and accurate estimation, MCMC methods empower economists to dynamically update hierarchical Bayesian models with new data, improving economic forecasts and policy analysis.
